claim: Cristae were discovered as characteristic elements of mitochondria more than 60 years ago.
source: More than 60 years ago, cristae were discovered as characteristic elements of mitochondria that harbor the protein complexes of oxidative phosphorylation, but how cristae are formed, remained an open question.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical scientific literature, as indicated by the reference to discoveries made more than 60 years ago.

claim: Cristae harbor the protein complexes of oxidative phosphorylation.
source: More than 60 years ago, cristae were discovered as characteristic elements of mitochondria that harbor the protein complexes of oxidative phosphorylation, but how cristae are formed, remained an open question.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cristae function.

claim: Formation of lamellar cristae depends on the mitochondrial fusion machinery.
source: Formation of lamellar cristae depends on the mitochondrial fusion machinery through a pathway that is required also for homeostasis of mitochondria and mitochondrial DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results presented in the manuscript, particularly the mgm1 mutant studies.

claim: The pathway for lamellar cristae formation is required for homeostasis of mitochondria and mitochondrial DNA.
source: Formation of lamellar cristae depends on the mitochondrial fusion machinery through a pathway that is required also for homeostasis of mitochondria and mitochondrial DNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mtDNA loss in various mutants.

claim: Tubular cristae are formed via invaginations of the inner boundary membrane by a pathway independent of the fusion machinery.
source: Tubular cristae are formed via invaginations of the inner boundary membrane by a pathway independent of the fusion machinery.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in dnm1Δmgm1Δ double mutants showing tubular cristae in the absence of fusion activity.

claim: Dimerization of the F1FO-ATP synthase is necessary for both pathways of crista formation.
source: Dimerization of the F1FO-ATP synthase and the presence of the MICOS complex are necessary for both pathways.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Su e deletion mutants showing altered crista structure.

claim: The presence of the MICOS complex is necessary for both pathways of crista formation.
source: Dimerization of the F1FO-ATP synthase and the presence of the MICOS complex are necessary for both pathways.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from MICOS deletion mutants.

claim: The key components of crista formation are conserved in structure and function throughout evolution.
source: The proposed hypothesis is suggested to apply also to higher eukaryotes, since the key components are conserved in structure and function throughout evolution.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of protein conservation and cited literature on mammalian homologs.

claim: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles undergoing continual fission and fusion.
source: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles undergoing continual fission and fusion (Bereiter-Hahn and Vöth, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The dynamics of mitochondria is essential for their function as well as maintenance, inheritance and integrity of their DNA.
source: The dynamics of mitochondria is essential for their function as well as maintenance, inheritance and integrity of their DNA (mtDNA).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mitochondria are involved in neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathies, metabolic diseases and cancer.
source: Recent research has revealed the involvement of this organelle in a multitude of human pathological conditions, including neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathies, metabolic diseases and cancer (Chan, 2012; Costa and Scorrano, 2012; Itoh et al., 2013; Mourier et al., 2014; Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012; Pickrell and Youle, 2013; Youle and van der Bliek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Mitochondrial ultrastructure is intimately linked to the function and homeostasis of this organelle.
source: Mitochondrial ultrastructure, also referred to as the mitochondrial architecture, is intimately linked to the function and homeostasis of this organelle, and has therefore been investigated in a large number of cell types, tissues and organisms (Fawcett, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: The inner membrane is composed of the inner boundary membrane and the crista membranes.
source: The inner membrane (IM) is composed of the inner boundary membrane (IBM) and the crista membranes.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about mitochondria.

claim: Cristae are invaginations of the inner membrane into the interior of the mitochondria.
source: The cristae are invaginations of the IM into the interior of the mitochondria (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by both text description and Figure 1 illustration.

claim: Cristae form lamellae in most cases, but tubules are also observed.
source: In most cases they form lamellae, but tubules are also observed (Fawcett, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Crista junctions join the cristae with the inner boundary membrane.
source: Crista junctions (CJs) join the cristae with the IBM.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: Crista junctions represent small ring or slot like openings that connect the intermembrane space with the intracrista space.
source: They represent small ring or slot like openings that connect the intermembrane space with the intracrista space.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about crista junctions.

claim: Cristae do not cross the matrix space completely, but they are closed by strongly bent crista rims.
source: Cristae do not cross the matrix space completely, but they are closed by strongly bent crista rims.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: Septa completely cross the matrix space and separate it into distinct compartments.
source: Septa completely cross the matrix space and separate it into distinct compartments.
evidence: This is based on structural observations and definitions.

claim: Septa are virtually absent in wild type cells, but are frequent in a variety of mutant cells.
source: They are virtually absent in wild type (WT) cells, but are frequent in a variety of mutant cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of Mgm1 in yeast leads to fragmentation of mitochondria and loss of respiration-dependent growth as well as of mtDNA.
source: Its deletion in yeast leads to fragmentation of mitochondria and loss of respiration-dependent growth as well as of mtDNA (Cipolat et al., 2004; Jones and Fangman, 1992; Meeusen et al., 2006; Song et al., 2009; Wong et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Previous EM analyses showed an altered inner membrane structure in Δmgm1 cells that includes the loss of cristae.
source: Previous EM analyses showed an altered IM structure in ∆mgm1 cells that includes the loss of cristae (Sesaki et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Quantitative EM of Δmgm1 cells revealed mitochondrial profiles that were mainly empty or contained one or a few septa.
source: Consistent with these observations, quantitative EM of ∆mgm1 cells revealed mitochondrial profiles that were mainly empty or contained one or a few septa.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The levels of mitochondrial respiratory components were strongly reduced in Δmgm1 cells.
source: Moreover, the levels of mitochondrial respiratory components were strongly reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In WT cells almost only cristae were present and no significant changes were observed upon exposure to 37°C and return to 25°C.
source: In WT cells almost only cristae were present and no significant changes were observed upon exposure to 37°C and return to 25°C (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: In mgm1-5 cells grown at 25°C, cristae made up about 70%.
source: In mgm1-5 cells grown at 25°C, cristae made up about 70%; apparently the temperature sensitive mutant was leaky.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Exposure of mgm1-5 cells to 37°C led to a drastic loss of cristae.
source: Exposure to 37°C and thus inactivation of Mgm1 led to a drastic loss of cristae (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Staining of mtDNA and test on respiratory competence revealed no loss of functional mtDNA upon exposure of mgm1-5 cells to 37°C for 25 min.
source: Indeed, staining of mtDNA and test on respiratory competence revealed no loss of functional mtDNA upon exposure to 37°C for 25 min (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Longer exposure (72 hr) of mgm1-5 cells to non-permissive temperature led to inhibition of cell growth on respiratory medium.
source: However, longer exposure (72 hr) of mgm1-5 cells to non-permissive temperature led to inhibition of cell growth on respiratory medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Upon return of the mgm1-5 cells to 25°C for 30 min cristae reappeared and septa were reduced.
source: Strikingly, upon return of the mgm1-5 cells to 25°C for 30 min cristae reappeared and septa were reduced, comparable to the situation before incubation at non-permissive temperature (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Mitochondrial respiratory complexes in both WT and mgm1-5 mutant remained intact during the temperature shifts.
source: Interestingly, mitochondrial respiratory complexes in both WT and mutant, as determined for Complex III and IV, remained intact during the temperature shifts (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Exposure of mgm1-5 cells to 37°C led to a decrease of lamellar and an increase of tubular cristae as compared to WT.
source: Notably, exposure of mgm1-5 cells to 37°C led to a decrease of lamellar and an increase of tubular cristae as compared to WT (Figure 2E and F; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 2E and F and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The formation of lamellar and tubular cristae relies on two different pathways.
source: These results show that the disappearance and reappearance of cristae are rapid and depend on functional Mgm1. We conclude that the formation of lamellar and tubular cristae relies on two different pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential effects on lamellar vs tubular cristae.

claim: Mgm1 plays a direct role in the formation and maintenance of lamellar but not of tubular cristae.
source: Moreover, Mgm1 plays a direct role in the formation and maintenance of lamellar but not of tubular cristae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing selective loss of lamellar cristae in mgm1 mutants.

claim: The majority of Mgm1 was localized to the OM/IBM and only about one third to the matrix/crista space.
source: Quantitative immuno-EM revealed that the majority of Mgm1 was localized to the OM/IBM and only about one third to the matrix/crista space (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mgm1 is present in two isoforms: l-Mgm1 and s-Mgm1.
source: Mgm1 is present in two isoforms (Shepard and Yaffe, 1999; Wong et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: l-Mgm1 contains a transmembrane helix that anchors it to the inner membrane.
source: l-Mgm1 contains a transmembrane helix that anchors it to the IM; in contrast, s-Mgm1 lacks the transmembrane helix and was reported to be present at the IBM or OM (Sesaki et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2000) and a short form of Opa1 was found to be co-localized with the OM fission machinery (Anand et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Both l-Mgm1 and s-Mgm1 forms are required for Mgm1 function in mitochondrial fusion.
source: Importantly, both l-Mgm1 and s-Mgm1 forms are required for Mgm1 function in mitochondrial fusion (DeVay et al., 2009; Zick et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: s-Mgm1 co-fractionated with the outer membrane marker Tom70.
source: Remarkably, s-Mgm1 co-fractionated with the outer membrane marker Tom70, indicating that it is associated with the outer membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Dimeric F1FO provides positive curvature to crista membranes.
source: Dimeric F1FO provides positive curvature to crista membranes (Dudkina et al., 2005; Strauss et al., 2008; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The subunits of the FO sector, Su e/Atp21 and Su g/Atp20, mediate the formation of F1FO dimers.
source: The subunits of the FO sector, Su e/Atp21 and Su g/Atp20, mediate the formation of F1FO dimers (Arnold et al., 1998; Habersetzer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Deletion of Su e or Su g leads to the formation of membrane sheets that are crossing the matrix space completely and to onion-like structures.
source: Deletion of Su e or Su g leads to the formation of membrane sheets that are crossing the matrix space completely and to onion-like structures.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: Fully assembled F1FO was found almost exclusively in the crista membranes of WT mitochondria.
source: We localized fully assembled F1FO by detection of its subunit F1β and found it almost exclusively in the crista membranes of WT mitochondria (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the Su e deletion mutant, the fraction of monomeric F1FO detected in the IBM was increased by a factor of three in comparison to WT.
source: In the Su e deletion mutant, however, the fraction of monomeric F1FO detected in the IBM was increased by a factor of three in comparison to WT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Su e was present in crista membranes of WT mitochondria.
source: Similar to F1β, Su e was present in crista membranes of WT mitochondria (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The MICOS complex is located in the mitochondrial inner membrane of yeast and higher eukaryotes.
source: The MICOS complex is located in the mitochondrial IM of yeast and higher eukaryotes, where it is required for the formation of CJs as well as the formation of contact sites with the OM.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: The MICOS complex is required for the formation of crista junctions.
source: The MICOS complex is located in the mitochondrial IM of yeast and higher eukaryotes, where it is required for the formation of CJs as well as the formation of contact sites with the OM.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: Mitochondria lacking Mic60 contain characteristic stacked membranes in the matrix that have no connections to the IBM.
source: Mitochondria lacking Mic60 contain characteristic stacked membranes in the matrix that have no connections to the IBM (Alkhaja et al., 2012; Darshi et al., 2011; Harner et al., 2011; Hoppins et al., 2011; Jans et al., 2013; John et al., 2005; Rabl et al., 2009; von der Malsburg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: F1β was found almost exclusively in the inner membrane stacks of Δmic60 mitochondria as in WT.
source: F1β was found almost exclusively in the IM stacks of ∆mic60 mitochondria as in WT (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The distribution of Cox5a between the IBM and the cristae in WT cells and between IBM and the internal membranes in the Δmic60 mutant was almost identical.
source: Likewise, the distribution of Cox5a between the IBM and the cristae in WT cells and between IBM and the internal membranes in the ∆mic60 mutant was almost identical (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mitochondria of the Δmic60 mutant are able to perform oxidative phosphorylation and thus maintain mtDNA.
source: Consistently, mitochondria of the ∆mic60 mutant are able to perform oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and thus maintain mtDNA.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of respiratory growth and mtDNA maintenance.

claim: Deletion of Su e did not lead to a reduction of MICOS subunits both during respiratory growth and fermentative growth.
source: Deletion of Su e did not lead to a reduction of MICOS subunits both during respiratory growth and fermentative growth (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The level of the assembled MICOS complex was strongly diminished in Δsu e cells.
source: The level of the assembled MICOS complex, however, was strongly diminished (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The MICOS subunit Mic10 was found to be strongly enriched at the sites where septa membranes meet the IBM and the bending of septa is strongest.
source: Interestingly, the MICOS subunit Mic10 was found to be strongly enriched at the sites where septa membranes meet the IBM and the bending of septa is strongest (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Dnm1 is an essential component of the fission machinery.
source: Dnm1 (in yeast)/Drp1 (in higher eukaryotes), a dynamin-related GTPase, is an essential component of the fission machinery.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Deletion of Dnm1 leads to the formation of a highly branched and interconnected mitochondrial network.
source: Its deletion leads to the formation of a highly branched and interconnected mitochondrial network (Bleazard et al., 1999; Otsuga et al., 1998; Smirnova et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Loss of Mgm1 in cells depleted of Dnm1 does not lead to loss of cristae.
source: Loss of Mgm1 in cells depleted of Dnm1 does not lead to loss of cristae (Sesaki et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Mitochondria in the Δdnm1 mutant are considerably enlarged, densely filled with vesicular profiles and short tubular cristae, while crista junctions are abundant along the IBM.
source: We observed that mitochondrial architecture differed significantly from that in WT. These mitochondria are considerably enlarged, densely filled with vesicular profiles and short tubular cristae, while CJs are abundant along the IBM (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In comparison to WT, the number of cristae with lamellar structure was found to be much lower in Δdnm1 mitochondria.
source: In comparison to WT, the number of cristae with lamellar structure was found to be much lower as highlighted by electron tomography.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 6B and Video 3.

claim: The vesicular profiles in Δdnm1 mitochondria mostly represent interconnected highly convoluted and branched tubular structures.
source: 3D reconstruction revealed that the vesicular profiles mostly represent interconnected highly convoluted and branched tubular structures (Figure 6B; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 6B and Video 3.

claim: Normal levels of components of OXPHOS as well as assembled MICOS and dimeric F1FO were present in Δdnm1 mitochondria.
source: Normal levels of components of OXPHOS as well as assembled MICOS and dimeric F1FO were present in these mitochondria (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The level of the assembled MICOS complex in the Δdnm1 mutant was significantly increased.
source: Notably, the level of the assembled MICOS complex in the ∆dnm1 mutant was significantly increased.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Growth of the Δdnm1 and Δdnm1Δmgm1 strains on non-fermentable carbon sources was similar.
source: Growth of the Δdnm1 and Δdnm1Δmgm1 strains on non-fermentable carbon sources was similar (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: On fermentable carbon source, the Δdnm1Δmgm1 double deletion mutant displayed a high rate of loss of mtDNA.
source: On fermentable carbon source, however, the double deletion mutant displayed a high rate of loss of mtDNA, pointing to a residual function of Mgm1 in mitochondria of the ∆dnm1 mutant (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The steady state levels of a number of mitochondrial proteins were similar in WT, Δdnm1, and Δdnm1Δmgm1 strains.
source: The steady state levels of a number of mitochondrial proteins were similar in WT, ∆dnm1, and Δdnm1Δmgm1 strains (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Lamellar cristae were not observed in mitochondria of the Δdnm1Δmgm1 mutant.
source: Strikingly, lamellar cristae were not observed in mitochondria of the Δdnm1Δmgm1 mutant (Figure 7D and E; Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and E and Video 4.

claim: Mgm1 appears to be essential for the formation of lamellar cristae, but is not required for the formation of tubular cristae and crista junctions.
source: Thus, Mgm1 appears to be essential for the formation of lamellar cristae, but is not required for the formation of tubular cristae and CJs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from the Δdnm1Δmgm1 mutant.

claim: Mitochondria in the Δdnm1Δmic60 mutant displayed a virtually complete absence of cristae and crista junctions.
source: We further investigated the mitochondria in the ∆dnm1∆mic60 mutant; they displayed a virtually complete absence of cristae and CJs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and tomographic data.

claim: Growth of Δdnm1Δmic60 cells was very slow on respiratory medium.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to the Δdnm1Δmgm1 mutant, growth of Δdnm1Δmic60 cells was very slow on respiratory medium (Figure 7A) and the rate of mtDNA loss was higher in this mutant, indicating that in the absence of fully functional Mgm1, MICOS and thereby CJs and tubular cristae contribute to maintenance of mtDNA (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Deletion of both Dnm1 and Su e resulted in cells that grew extremely slowly on non-fermentable carbon source.
source: Deletion of both Dnm1 and Su e resulted in cells that grew extremely slowly on non-fermentable carbon source (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Mitochondria in Δdnm1Δsu e cells contained many highly branched septa and multi-layered onion-like profiles.
source: Mitochondria contained many highly branched septa and multi-layered onion-like profiles (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: mtDNA was lost at a high rate in Δdnm1Δsu e cells.
source: In addition, mtDNA was lost at a high rate, indicating that dimeric F1FO is important for maintenance of mtDNA when Mgm1 has no obvious role (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mitochondria in the Δdnm1Δmgm1Δmic60 and the Δdnm1Δsu eΔmic60 triple mutants showed even more severe ultrastructural alterations than the double mutants.
source: Strikingly, mitochondria in the Δdnm1Δmgm1Δmic60 and the Δdnm1Δsu eΔmic60 triple mutants showed even more severe ultrastructural alterations than the Δdnm1Δmgm1, Δdnm1Δmic60, or Δdnm1Δsu e double mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Approximately 50% of mitochondrial profiles in Δdnm1Δmgm1Δmic60 and Δdnm1Δsu eΔmic60 triple mutants were completely empty.
source: Fewer internal sheet-like membranes were present and approximately 50% of mitochondrial profiles were completely empty (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Loss of mtDNA in the Δdnm1Δmgm1Δmic60 triple mutant was particularly high.
source: Loss of mtDNA in the Δdnm1Δmgm1Δmic60 triple mutant was particularly high (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Recent experiments with reconstituted vesicles have revealed that Mgm1 mediates membrane bending.
source: Very interestingly, recent experiments with reconstituted vesicles have revealed that Mgm1 mediates membrane bending (Rujiviphat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Mitochondria isolated from mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking functional Opa1 lacked lamellar cristae and instead contained short tubular-type cristae.
source: Most interestingly, a study on the role of Opa1 in mitochondrial cristae remodeling showed that mitochondria isolated from mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking functional Opa1 lacked lamellar cristae; instead, these mitochondria contained short tubular-type cristae (Frezza et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Oligomeric forms of the MICOS subunit Mic10 can induce membrane curvature in vitro.
source: Interestingly, oligomeric forms of the MICOS subunit Mic10 can induce membrane curvature in vitro and were suggested to form CJs in vivo (Barbot et al., 2015; Bohnert et al., 2015; Milenkovic and Larsson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Regular helical zipper-like structures of presumably dimeric F1FO were observed at the surface of the tubular cristae of the protist Paramecium multimicronucleatum by scanning EM.
source: Interestingly, regular helical zipper-like structures of presumably dimeric F1FO were observed at the surface of the tubular cristae of the protist Paramecium multimicronucleatum by scanning EM (Allen et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: mtDNA, condensed in nucleoids, was reported to be bound to crista membranes, possibly to crista rims.
source: In fact, mtDNA, condensed in nucleoids, was reported to be bound to crista membranes, possibly to crista rims (Kopek et al., 2012; Kukat and Larsson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Lamellar cristae dominate in pancreatic cells and hepatocytes.
source: For example, lamellar cristae dominate in pancreatic cells and hepatocytes, whereas in steroidogenic cells tubular cristae are the principle architectural feature.
evidence: This is based on published observations of mitochondrial ultrastructure in different cell types.

claim: In steroidogenic cells tubular cristae are the principle architectural feature.
source: For example, lamellar cristae dominate in pancreatic cells and hepatocytes, whereas in steroidogenic cells tubular cristae are the principle architectural feature.
evidence: This is based on published observations of mitochondrial ultrastructure in different cell types.

claim: A mixed situation of lamellar and tubular cristae prevails in certain types of muscle cells.
source: A mixed situation prevails in certain types of muscle cells where both lamellar and tubular profiles can be recognized (Blinzinger et al., 1965; Fawcett, 1981; Hanaki et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Tomographic reconstruction of cerebellar neuronal cells revealed lamellar and tubular cristae that are regularly connected by sites of fusion.
source: Such a study has been performed with cerebellar neuronal cells and revealed lamellar and tubular cristae that are regularly connected by sites of fusion (Perkins et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Differentiation of isolated zona glomerulosa cells of rat adrenal cortex triggered by treatment with adrenocorticotropic hormone leads to a drastic change of the corticoid hormones synthesized and to a concomitant transformation of the crista structure from mainly lamellar-tubular to tubular-convolute.
source: Furthermore, the differentiation of isolated zona glomerulosa cells of rat adrenal cortex triggered by treatment with adrenocorticotropic hormone leads to a drastic change of the corticoid hormones synthesized and to a concomitant transformation of the crista structure from mainly "lamellar-tubular" to "tubular-convolute" (Andreis et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Steroidogenesis in human trophoblasts was reported to be dependent on the activity of Opa1.
source: Interestingly, steroidogenesis in human trophoblasts was reported to be dependent on the activity of Opa1. During developmental induction of the steroidogenic pathway, Opa1 levels decreased and steroid formation increased. Manipulations of cells to increase Opa1 levels led to decreased efficiency of steroidogenesis. At the same time, crista structure was observed to be remodeled (Wasilewski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.
